rv.q: Jones is superb: ridiculous, loudly self-pitying, sarcastic — and desolate.
It returns us to the great, mournful spirit of Chekhov’s tale about unrequited love, ageing and disappointment in middle-age, while giving it a sleeker, modern beat.

Like so many good versions of classics, Conor McPherson’s new adaptation feels almost impossibly contemporary in the way it packs so much lust, wit, rage and regret into its brisk but unhurried two and a half hours.
The alchemy of this retooled Vanya, combining a top-notch creative team with serious actors who are currently having A Moment, works brilliantly.
This version finds a sweet spot between companionable chuckles and icy despair.
Ian Rickson's production is polished to a high shine... everything about it gleams, almost too much; it's too controlled, too tidy.
Assisted by a nuanced, if occasionally foul-mouthed new version by Conor McPherson, again he delivers a bravura performance, even more affecting this time round.
In Eleazar, Rickson's found gold.
Toby Jones’s wonderfully funny Vanya is the real pay-off.

Crumpled with disillusion, Toby Jones is a very fine Vanya: he does something truly Chekhovian in making the difference between comic and sad look like a trick of the light, and as a quizzical crosspatch is unusual in making his character’s foray into farcical violence look convincing.
Both Wood and Eleazar allow their characters to develop slowly: that stealth is essential to make sense of Sonya’s beautiful epilogue about the reversion of routine and mankind’s acceptance of fate.
Every single player here evokes their character's ennui terrifically – but it is so dimly lit, the staging so staid, the pace so unhurried, that the ennui is catching.
This production of Uncle Vanya makes it seem as accessible as a TV drama, without ever betraying the great, melancholy, insightful soul that has made the play last for as long as it has.
It’s a superlative collective performance from the cast – many of us will be lucky if we see a better one in our lifetimes.
This richly detailed production is housed within a stunning set by Rae Smith, gorgeously lit by Bruno Poet and hauntingly scored by composer Stephen Warbeck.
This is certainly no cliched production.

Overall, this new version of Uncle Vanya is entertaining ,playing up and introducing comic moments wherever possible but keeping much of the spirit of Chekhov, while the new elements give it a more contemporary edge.
Around the edges of this slightly wonky production are several strong performances.
Judged by Rickson own past record, this only intermittently touching and funny production is a disappointment.
Rickson’s production, with its first-rate cast and delicately altered script, offer up a fantastic version of this well-loved classic.
Toby Jones delivers an acting masterclass.
In my opinion it managed to capture the best of the theatre and the cinema experience.
The lack of energy may be the biggest tragedy for some, but that may well be the point in this otherwise powerfully performed, character-driven musing on existentialism.
But the new ideas attached to this classic feel like woolly thinking and the evening falls between the two stools of convention and invention.

cn.t: Rickson's exquisite production draws acclaim for its perfectly balanced tragicomedy, with Toby Jones's rumpled Vanya and McPherson's modernized adaptation earning particular praise, though a few critics find it suffocating or uneven.
